extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, newsroom photo editors, and newspaper editors/journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for ethical photojournalism focused on image manipulation, newsroom verification, and editorial response when a published photograph is altered. Covers expectations for photographers, editors, and news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No image manipulation / do not deceive readers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not ever a good time for such manipulation; being in the desert away from your readers does not mean you have free license to deceive them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple practitioners emphasize that altering photos to change what actually occurred is unacceptable. The piece quotes Maria Mann and Vincent LaForet: manipulation is never appropriate and stands as deception of readers. This is presented as a clear prohibition rather than a nuanced allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain credibility and trust with readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility is all that we have; if readers can’t count on honesty from us, we have nothing left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors frame credibility as the core asset of journalism; breaches of photographic truth harm journalists collectively. The article uses this principle to justify strong remedial action and to stress the long-term costs of deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swift investigation and decisive editorial action
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should investigate apparent breaches promptly and take decisive action (example: Walski was investigated and fired).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Los Angeles Times posted an editors note, investigated the image, and fired the photographer. The article presents speed and decisiveness as appropriate newsroom responses to confirmed manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish corrections and be transparent (publish originals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish a correction and provide full transparency about the breach, including publishing the originals alongside the altered image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribune planned a correction and the Times/Courant published the two originals and the altered composite to inform readers. Transparency is shown as a remediation step to restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough verification and forensic scrutiny of suspect images
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspected manipulations should be examined carefully (example: 600% magnification in Photoshop revealed duplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Courant employee's discovery and subsequent magnified Photoshop inspection illustrate practical verification steps newsrooms should use to detect composites and manipulations before or after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the benefit of the doubt but gather full information
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may initially give a photographer benefit of the doubt, but must promptly collect information and verify the photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colin Crawford recounts sending the photographer 'the benefit of the doubt' and gathering information; the article frames this as a balanced editorial posture—sympathetic but investigative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal hardship (fatigue/stress) is not an acceptable excuse for deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatigue and horrific conditions may explain lapses, but do not excuse violating ethical standards; there is 'no acceptable explanation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleagues express sympathy for the photographer's exhausted state but leaders and peers consistently reject exhaustion as a justification for manipulation, emphasizing accountability despite context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and photo directors must uphold and enforce ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership responsibility includes enforcing standards, acting when trust is violated, and communicating actions to staff and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes from Colin Crawford and other managing editors justify the firing and stress that protecting organizational integrity requires enforcement even when consequences are painful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be vigilant about modern-technology temptations and train staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should be continually vigilant and aware of the temptation that modern technology offers and provide ethics training and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article counsels ongoing vigilance and points to the role of training (Poynter’s programs referenced) and awareness to prevent lapses triggered by easy digital manipulation tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept responsibility and apologize, but expect consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A photographer should accept responsibility and apologize for breaches; apology does not eliminate professional consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walski’s 214-word apology is cited as taking responsibility, yet the paper still fired him—demonstrating that contrition is necessary but insufficient to avoid disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal distribution and syndication require extra checks
rubrics_metrics.description: When images are distributed across properties (e.g., via internal services like Newscom), errors/misconduct can propagate widely and require robust checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The image was shared with Tribune properties and used prominently by other papers; the piece implies that wider distribution amplifies harm and therefore calls for verification procedures before syndication.
